questions.q: Per the Google SRE book's published definition used in this lesson, which of the following is a defining property of toil?
options: It must involve writing code of any kind
It is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and scales linearly with service growth
It only occurs during a declared incident
It is any task that takes longer than one hour to complete
questions.explain: Toil has a specific, narrow definition: manual, repetitive, automatable in principle, tactical/reactive rather than strategic, leaving no lasting improvement, and growing in direct proportion to service or traffic growth.

questions.q: Why is writing a postmortem or designing a new alerting strategy NOT considered toil under this definition, even though both take real time?
options: Because they are performed by managers rather than engineers
Because they produce lasting improvements to the system and don't recur identically each time, unlike toil
Because they are automatable by a script
Because they only take a few minutes to complete
questions.explain: Toil is specifically devoid of enduring value and recurs. A postmortem or a new alerting strategy leaves the system in a permanently better state, which disqualifies it from the toil definition even though it takes effort.

questions.q: Why does toil become a serious engineering problem specifically as an organization scales from ten services to two hundred?
options: Toil scales linearly with service growth while headcount grows sub-linearly at best, so the proportion of manual work keeps increasing unless it's automated away
Toil automatically disappears once an organization passes fifty services
Because larger organizations are legally required to hire more SREs
Toil has nothing to do with the number of services an organization runs
questions.explain: Headcount never scales linearly with services or traffic because hiring is slow and expensive. If toil isn't automated away, SREs end up spending an ever-growing share of their time on manual firefighting instead of preventive engineering.

questions.q: What does the Google SRE book's '50% rule' specify, and how is it treated operationally according to this lesson?
options: It suggests SREs take 50% of their vacation days as toil-reduction time; it is rarely tracked
It caps SRE time spent on toil at roughly 50%, with the rest reserved for engineering project work; it's tracked as measured data and acted on, not treated as a motivational slogan
It requires exactly 50% of all engineers company-wide to be dedicated SREs
It limits error budgets to 50% of the SLO
questions.explain: The 50% rule caps toil's share of an SRE team's time. Teams that take it seriously measure and report this percentage and treat consistently exceeding it as a signal requiring action, the same way burn rate drives error budget decisions.

questions.q: What is the organizational tell, per this lesson, that a company genuinely treats toil reduction as an engineering priority rather than an aspiration?
options: Toil reduction is funded with explicit sprint capacity or headcount and tracked through periodic toil audits, rather than squeezed in during slow weeks
Toil is mentioned once in an onboarding document and never discussed again
Engineers are asked to volunteer personal time outside work hours to reduce toil
The company outsources all toil-heavy work to an unrelated vendor with no internal tracking
questions.explain: Mature SRE organizations run quarterly toil audits, measure toil as a percentage of time the same way they track SLO compliance, and allocate real budget or headcount to automate the highest-volume manual processes.
